title: How the diesel price spike is rippling through nearly every part of the economy
summary: PBS on the 2026 diesel spike: globally set prices driven by the Iran war and Russian export ban, ripple effects on farms and freight, and why an export ban would backfire.

assertions.quote: the price of diesel we pay at the pump for gasoline for that matter, is set in a global market

verdicts.note: Crude is the bulk of the pump price and is set in a world market; domestic policy moves retail prices only at the margin.

Pump prices tracked crude under both administrations: WTI 91.64 to 114.84 (Feb-Jun 2022) with gasoline 3.517 to 4.929, WTI 64.51 to 102.13 (Feb-May 2026) with gasoline 2.908 to 4.479, and the 2025 decline of WTI to 57.97 with gasoline easing to 2.894; co-movement supports the claim but cannot exclude policy effects on crude itself.

assertions.quote: coming from disruptions in first, the Arabian Gulf area due to the war with Iran
Russia has had to ban its exports of diesel because the Ukrainians have been successful at destroying the refineries
it's important, it's important for the Federal Reserve and macroeconomists as an inflation risk
But then the prices would rise again because refiners would reduce their production of diesel.

verdicts.note: Energy economists across the spectrum reached the same conclusion on 2022 export-ban proposals: trapped supply lowers Gulf Coast prices for weeks, then refinery cuts and higher world prices reverse it.

assertions.quote: since this administration came in from tariffs when the prices plummeted. We never recruit. We ran more and fertilizer prices went through the roof

verdicts.note: Chinese retaliation collapsed US soybean exports in 2025 and tariffs on imported fertilizer raised input costs, both documented in USDA data.
